newsitem.title: GERMANY: Top bankers may have ot testify in Schneider trial.
newsitem.headline: Top bankers may have ot testify in Schneider trial.

text.p: Top German bankers may have to testify in the trial of real estate tycoon Juergen Schneider to respond to his allegations that they shared blame for the collapse of his property empire, a prosecutor said on Thursday.

Dieter Haike, one of two prosecutors handling Germany's biggest corporate fraud scandal, told Reuters the trial would now adress Schneider's allegations that his creditor banks knew his loan requests were backed by forged or incorrect documents.
Asked whether management board members of the banks, which include market leaders Deutsche Bank AG and Dresdner Bank AG, might be called to testify, Haike said:

"Everyone who was involved with the matter, and you know that loans of this size are approved at management board level, will possibly be heard when the issue is to find out what they thought and what reasons can they give.
"You can't conclude a case like this without having questioned a loan processor."

Schneider, 63, once one of Germany's most celebrated entrepreneurs, has been on trial since Monday for alleged fraud relating to the collapse of his group under more than five billion marks ($2.9 billion) of debt in 1994.
The trial entered its second day on Thursday and is due to resume next Tuesday.
He has admitted presenting banks with forged bills, rental contracts and blueprints to gain credit but added that the banks must have been aware of this.
Schneider has accused them of tacitly accepting the irregularities to circumvent strict laws on property financing because they, like he, were convinced the projects would be profitable.
The banks have consistently denied the allegations and prosecutors have said they found no evidence of wrongdoing by banks even though they maintain serious mistakes were made.
A Deutsche spokesman on Thursday declined fresh comment on Schneider's accusations and said he had no knowledge of whether any officials from the bank had been called to testify.
Haike said: "We're in a subjective area and we have to assess it. We have to assess his statement that the banks knew what was happening."
If it emerged that the banks did collude with Schneider then that could affect his sentence, Haike said.
Schneider faces a theoretical maximum sentence of 15 years for the charges of credit fraud and serious fraud but any sentence is expected to be far shorter.
The case could prove embarrassing for the banks which faced public outrage in 1994 at the apparent ease with which they doled out billions.
They financed what Schneider has called his dream to restore historic charm to German cities with stylish hotels and shopping malls.
The tycoon became the toast of German business during the post-unification property boom but his group crumbled because his rental income was too low to repay his mounting debts.

The group filed for bankruptcy shortly after Schneider and his wife Claudia disappeared in April 1994, sparking an international manhunt. They were arrested in Miami, Florida, one year later and extradited to Germany in 1996.
